In the current version, reference text in the main judge is opt-in only, behind an environment switch (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/evaluators/question.py`).

merges.why: Comparing a judge with and without added reference text before adopting it is a special case of changing a check only after a paired trial. The finding that such text can make a judge worse is kept in the statement.

merges.statement: Make every check and audit list, item by item, what it read and skipped, and treat the rest as unchecked until covered: a clean result proves only what was read.

folded_records.statement: A check vouches only for what it reads, so have each one list what it read, item by item, and treat everything outside its reach as unchecked.
folded_records.detail: In the reading course, a semantic check that collected only the choice questions missed breaches in narrated text twice (`grade3-reading/artifacts/AlphaRead-QC-Checklist-v2-2026-09-04.md`), an asset validator that walks only authored strings could not see four missing clips whose paths are built at run time (`grade3-reading/artifacts/peter-pan-standing-2026-09-11/VISUAL-QA-2026-09-11.md`), and an outside audit script never read the fields where one leak sat (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-inceptbench-2026-09-30/REGISTER.md`). People found 26 problems on lessons whose gate was green at review time; every check in the 18-script battery read authored JSON or JSX text, never a rendered page, and the findings that kept recurring were visible only on the rendered page or in the language (`grade3-reading/artifacts/cert-layer/AUTOMATED-CHECKS-ROADMAP-2026-08-31.md`). Of 10 findings in one register, 6 needed a sequence of actions or were not visual, so a cold screenshot could not judge them, and a screenshot judge's pass on a screen that never showed the defect's own controls was no evidence the fix held (`grade3-reading/artifacts/cert-layer/VISION-QA-CALIBRATION-2026-08-31.md`). A count check asked only whether the count matched, never whether the new item was the right one, and was bumped every round; the proposed fix has it list what was added or removed (`grade3-reading/artifacts/peter-pan-standing-2026-09-11/GAPS-2026-09-11.md`).

merges.why: These are one rule in two wordings: a clean result vouches only for what the check read. One record has each check list what it read, item by item rather than as a count. The other has it name what it did not read and where its scope ends, and cover what lies beyond. Both are the same declaration of scope, with everything outside it treated as unchecked. Neither record was on record. The kept record sits in the making-and-reviewing group, which fits checks of every kind better than the AI-judges group the folded one was filed under.

merges.statement: Before filing or fixing a finding, confirm it on the current, settled, live build, test the check that raised it on clean content, and publish how many were withdrawn.

folded_records.statement: Before filing a fault in a lesson, confirm it on the full-size, settled screen, check nobody asked for it, and rule out the test environment.
folded_records.detail: The reading course's quality gates add a filing gate before any finding ships, after findings of its own went wrong: three 'nothing happened' blockers were feedback rendering in the other column, a hung media-capture call in a headless browser produced a false dead end, and a team was once told to revert to a design that had been explicitly rejected (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/key-quality-gates.md`, lines 118-137). On the first uncalibrated sweep, 4 of 6 blockers were retracted, and publishing that rate is what made the second sweep trustworthy. The course's agent spec adds that a finding resting on a checkable factual error damages the audit more than the package. Confirm a fault with the whole page watched over time and designed timers waited out, and publish how many findings were withdrawn.

merges.why: Both say a finding is not a fact until it is confirmed on the real, current lesson, because many findings turn out false or stale. One puts that gate before filing: a settled, full-size screen, not a test-environment artifact, not a design that was asked for, and the number withdrawn published. The other puts it before fixing: the current build, and the check that raised the finding tried on clean content. Filing is one way of acting on a finding, so the filing rule is a special case. Neither record was on record. one-manual-read-is-a-floor and count-only-independent-agreement stay apart, because they ask for a second independent read and for agreement between independent methods, not for confirmation on the build.

merges.statement: Review in rounds, each through a new lens and again after every change, fixes and display code included, and stop only after two rounds in a row find nothing new.

folded_records.statement: Stop reviewing a layer only after two rounds in a row find nothing new.
folded_records.detail: The course-plan gauntlet advances a candidate layer by layer, and each layer must go dry, two consecutive rounds with zero new findings, before the next; every finding and its repair is logged in a promotion ledger (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/train-teacher/references/gauntlet-spec.md`). One round with no findings is not enough on its own.

merges.why: The second record is the first record's stopping rule, stated more strictly. One reviews until a fresh round finds nothing critical. The other stops a layer only after two rounds in a row find nothing new, and says one dry round is not enough. Kept apart, the two would give conflicting stop rules. The merged statement keeps the new lens each round and the re-review after every change, and takes the stricter two-round stop. Neither record was on record. check-the-design-against-its-target stays apart, because it names a specific lens to use when rounds turn cosmetic.

merges.statement: Judge content by what the delivered player shows, checking files, the student's live experience and course claims apart, and count an authored element or gate only once seen working.

folded_records.statement: Check the content files, what a student experiences when the lesson runs, and the claims made about the course separately, because passing one does not show the others pass.
folded_records.detail: An analysis of gaps in an automated content evaluator separates criteria into three rings: what can be checked in the course and lesson files, runtime behaviour on a live walkthrough of the student's seat, and the integrity of the package and its claims; it says the evaluator should not overclaim runtime behaviour or package truth. A review of a course-schema package records that schema validity is a document-integrity floor only, never a verdict on course quality, readiness for children or outcomes.

merges.why: Both say that passing the files does not show the delivered lesson works. One judges content by what the player shows and does, not by its data. The other checks the content files, the live experience and the claims about the course as separate layers, because passing one does not show the others pass. The first is the files-against-experience case of the second, so the merged statement keeps the claims layer as well. Neither record was on record. review-as-a-student (on record) stays apart, because it is about which mode to review in. show-the-sequence-dont-claim-it also stays apart, because it names what a knowledge sequence must visibly contain.

merges.statement: Settle in code everything code can decide, such as format, parts and key validity, before a judge sees the item, then give the judge those results as binding facts.

folded_records.statement: Settle in code everything with a mechanical verdict before a judge sees the item, and keep judgment for what needs interpretation.
folded_records.detail: An analysis of two benchmark runs found factual-accuracy failures such as four identical options and keys that did not match the options, and listed "No validation that correct answer is actually in the options" among what was lacking, though the fix it chose was few-shot examples (`icloud-work/incept/nova_forge/archive/old_docs/platform/PATTERN_ANALYSIS_RESULTS.md`). A later report on a math generator, after occasional key mismatches in word problems, planned a deterministic arithmetic verifier to reject any item whose computed answer differs from its key (`icloud-work/incept/nova_forge/qwen3-math/docs/inceptml_full_report.md`). Neither file measures a check in code. Mechanical verdicts include the key being among the options, a computed answer or known fact matching the key, required parts and fields being present, a link resolving and a hash matching.

folded_records.statement: Check in code whatever code can decide, because neither a prompt instruction nor a model judge guarantees it.
folded_records.detail: An AP evaluator left multiple-select questions with a single keyed answer to its model, which let some through; a check in code before the model call made them fail every time (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/archive/MSQ_FIX_RESULTS.md`). Telling the writer to keep primary sources short did not keep them short (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/archive/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS_2026-02-18.md`), and a banned-words list in the prompt had no detection or rejection behind it, so it was only advisory (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/archive/improvement_plan_prompts.md`). A fine-tuned model also put a Chinese word into an English question set (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/data/model_findings.md`), a slip a check in code would find. What code can decide includes how many answers are keyed and how long a source runs.

merges.why: All three say the same thing: whatever code can decide is checked in code, because no prompt and no model judge guarantees it. The kept record says that and also makes the code results binding on the judge, so the other two are subsets of it. None is on_record.

merges.statement: Bind each question to the exact text it was written and checked against, and confirm that pairing on the delivered form as a blocking check of its own.

folded_records.statement: Check, as a blocking step of its own on the assembled form, that each item and the passage it is shown with are about the same thing.
folded_records.detail: An audit of a live Grade 3 course found a mastery form with five items bound to one passage, four of them written for a different topic and unanswerable as rendered: the class of defect that passes item evaluations but fails the course. Three methods with no model in them converged on it, an item-level overlap screen, a per-passage overlap-ratio outlier test and a direct read, after an any-overlap aggregate had first returned a false all-clear because one shared word bridged the two topics. The report's doctrine is to gate form and passage coherence with a deterministic check and never to assume an item-quality pass means the passage and the question are about the same thing. An item judged on its own can pass while it sits on the wrong passage.

merges.why: Both cover the same failure, a question shipped next to a passage it was not made for. Both give the same fix: check the question-passage pairing on the assembled, delivered form, because checking each item alone misses it. Neither is on_record.

merges.statement: Hard-block in code only what code detects reliably, keep keyword and length counts advisory, and check quality and correctness separately, since a well-formed item can be weak or wrong.

folded_records.statement: A well-formed item is not a correct one; check structure and content separately, because fixing the form didn't fix the content.
folded_records.detail: When examples taught a missing question-set format in the AP question work, its pass rate rose from 0% to 12%: the writer now produced three questions, a stimulus and every required field, but factual accuracy and stimulus quality still failed 88% of the time (`icloud-work/ML learnings/mcq_set_journey.md`). The note's own reading was that format and quality are different problems. The research summary adds that a grammar can force a well-formed date field but not the right date (`icloud-work/ML learnings/research_rag_factual_grounding.md`), and that content quality, not structural compliance, is what separates larger writers from smaller ones (`icloud-work/ML learnings/research_model_size_vs_data_quality.md`).

merges.why: The kept record already ends with the merged record's whole point: a valid shape says nothing about content, so judge content separately. The merged record is that one clause on its own, a special case. Neither is on_record.

merges.statement: Sweep everything a student is served, as it renders, for authoring leftovers such as working notes, markup tokens, escaped characters and placeholder codes, which instructions alone don't prevent.

folded_records.statement: Keep a writer's working notes out of what learners see and check the delivered text for them, because an instruction alone does not stop notes from leaking.
folded_records.detail: One prompt asked the explanation writer for step-by-step analysis notes and the final explanation in the same response, adding 'Do not include headers or titles in the explanation'. The code returned the model's text unparsed, and explanations were written after the quality checks and never checked. 22 of 60 delivered explanations (18 of 25, 3 of 16 and 1 of 19 by quiz) begin with '#' note headers such as '# Initial Analysis', the converted delivery files carry the same 22, and some leaked notes tell students the question is 'fundamentally flawed'.

merges.why: Working notes left in the delivered text are one kind of authoring leftover. Both records call for the same check: scan the text students actually get rather than trust the instruction that produced it. Neither is on_record.

merges.statement: Use a few vetted examples to show a writer an item's form, never its facts, since it copies their content and flaws: take them from other topics, stripped to structure.

folded_records.statement: Show the writer three to five verified examples of the item type, taken from other topics so that it copies the form but not the content.
folded_records.detail: In an A/B on AP question sets, the generator was shown 3 to 5 exemplars that had scored 1.0 with the grader, drawn from a pool of 669 and chosen so their standard differed from the target's. The pass rate rose from 3.3% to 26.7% and answer balance went from 0 to 30/30, which suggests about 30 sets, so the gain is a handful of items.

merges.why: Both records give the same rule. A writer copies the content of any example it is shown, so examples should be verified and used only for an item's form. The other-topics record is one measured case of that rule. The statement keeps its advice to take examples from other topics and adds the broader record's step of stripping them to structure, because off-topic examples once carried their content into new items. Neither record was on record before this run.

merges.statement: Warnings and bans don't reliably steer a writer: some invite the error they name, exact trap lists help without removing it, unchecked bans stay advisory; change what it's given instead.

folded_records.statement: Whether warnings steer a writer is disputed: naming the exact words and traps to avoid went with higher pass rates without removing the error.
folded_records.detail: In one fine-tuned model's runs, adding a forbidden list to the essay prompt raised that type's pass rate by 15.9 points over the previous gate, and the findings say the list genuinely helped (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/data/model_findings.md`). Across six runs in an archived analysis of the generator's prompt versions, concrete bad examples showed a strong positive correlation with passing (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/archive/VERSION_ANALYSIS.md`). A banned-words list in another version of the prompts had no detection or rejection behind it and was only advisory (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/archive/improvement_plan_prompts.md`).

merges.why: Both records ask one question: do warnings and bans in a prompt steer a writer? One says no. The other holds the evidence against that: exact trap lists went with higher pass rates without removing the error, and a ban list nothing checked stayed advisory. The house keeps a contradicted learning as one record with its counter-evidence in against, so the two become one statement that covers both sides. The kept record may need contested status. Neither record was on record before this run.

merges.statement: A mastery gate needs enough items: on four or five items a 90% bar demands a perfect score, so check each bar against the real item count, again after cuts.

folded_records.statement: A percentage bar needs enough items to mean anything: on a test of only a few items, a 90% bar can't be applied.
folded_records.detail: An evaluation of a live Grade 3 course scored its mastery truthfulness 1 of 5, and one reason was that two 4-5 item tests could not be gated, since there is no 90% of 4 (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0058-eval-reading-explorers-g3-allqtypes.qmd`). The same line lists the other reasons: the threshold was declared but not enforced, lesson tests carried no threshold, and there was no retry on parallel forms.

merges.why: Both records give the same rule, that a percentage mastery bar needs enough items, and both cite the same Grade 3 evaluation of 4-5 item tests that could not be gated at 90%. The percentage record is a narrower restatement of the gate record, which already includes the four-or-five-item case. Neither record was on record before this run.

merges.statement: List excerpts from a text in the order they occur in it, since a reordered list can make a line seem to belong to the wrong speaker or moment.

folded_records.statement: When students choose from excerpts of a text, list the excerpts in the order they appear in the text.
folded_records.detail: A validator added to the reading project's question rules on 30 September 2026 fails a tappable sentence list that is not offered in the order its sentences occur in the passage. It came from a pinned defect: a clue list put last a line that sits earlier in the story, so a child tapping the list in order was sent backward through the scene. The fix is mechanical, by a tool that reorders the list and remaps its keys.

merges.why: Both give one rule for lines offered from a text, usually tap lists students choose from: keep them in the text's order. One record adds the reason (a moved line reads as the wrong speaker or moment), and the other adds the choosing context. Both come from the same reading project's story-order validator. The kept record is the more general one and has the measured example.

merges.statement: Anything taught needs graded work where learners produce it, as picking, recognising, mentioning or echoing it never counts, and no earlier check may use a taught word as its answer.

folded_records.statement: Every taught word needs at least one graded task in which the student must produce it, since mentioning or recognising it doesn't count.
folded_records.detail: An arc audit of a reading course found two taught words acquired but never required by any graded surface, and the course adopted a rule that every taught word needs one such use. The definition was then sharpened to graded usage, not mention: the student produces the word in an evaluative sentence, and multiple-choice recognition alone, however many options, never counts. The graded task can be the independent task, and no earlier check should use the taught word as an answer.

merges.why: The taught-word record is the vocabulary case of the general production rule. It cites the same vocabulary rulings and quotes: graded usage, not mention, and recognition never counts however many options there are. Its one extra point, keeping a taught word out of earlier checks' answers, is carried into the statement.

merges.statement: Each wrong option must attract a student who misunderstood, and only the tested knowledge or the text may rule it out, never common sense or surface cues.

folded_records.statement: Build each wrong option so that only a reader of the text can reject it, such as a real detail of the text with one element changed.
folded_records.detail: The reading project's writer rules build distractors from real passage details with the wrong actor, stage, effect, cause or claim swapped in, require that rejecting one means returning to a specific sentence, and forbid absurd ones, which leak the key by elimination. When the passage takes a specific or counter-typical stance, the textbook generalization becomes a deliberate wrong option, and the blind grader treats a key that matches the textbook default as a general-knowledge leak. A lesson audit found distractors that were self-declared filler, and the item standard fails a set of one obvious right answer and 3 throwaways. Each wrong option should rest on a different misreading.

merges.why: For a question on a text, the tested knowledge is the text, so 'only a reader can reject it' is the text case of 'only the tested knowledge can reject it'. Both records also forbid absurd, easily dropped options and filler. Close records that say something different stay separate: named misconceptions with corrective feedback, shortcut-catching options, options true elsewhere in the text, and taught-word options for word checks, which adds an alignment rule.

merges.statement: No correct answer in a set may contradict another, and what one step marks right or teaches must still hold in the next, so check the whole set.

folded_records.statement: In a task done in steps, what one step marks right must still count when the student carries it into the next step.
folded_records.detail: Hand reviews of reading lessons found write-ups whose steps contradicted each other. In one, Step 4's rubric refused words that Step 3 had just keyed as right; in another, Step 4 marked Step 3's answer unpredictably; in a third, the early steps sent students away from the paragraph holding the clue a later step required them to copy; and in a fourth, one step said a paragraph was not the ending and the next marked a line from it as the ending. In each case the student who followed the method as taught was the one who failed.

merges.why: A later step that refuses what an earlier step marked right, or contradicts what it taught, is one part of a set contradicting another. That makes the stepped-task record a special case of set agreement. The more general record is kept, and the step cases are written into the statement. Define-what-counts-once stays separate because its point is keeping one acceptance rule per answer.

merges.statement: An item, its options, hints and pointers may require only what the student has met by then on every path, common knowledge, or what the item or reference materials supply.

folded_records.statement: A question, its options and hints, and any line pointing to other material may depend only on what the student has met by then, along every path leading there.
folded_records.detail: The reading project's forward-reference check flags any question, option or hint on a page that depends on a concrete story noun the child has not read yet, one that first appears after that page or nowhere in the lesson (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0234-misc-artifacts-gate-eval-checks-recovery.qmd`). When a later course's closing questions named an earlier course's story as their link, the earlier lessons' closing sentences stopped being free choices: they had to land the ideas those questions point at, or the questions would point at content the child never met (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0225-g3-closing-questions-adoption-2026-09-24.qmd`). This holds for lines pointing to earlier or later material, and where the order isn't known such a line must stay vague, as in "earlier in the course".

merges.why: Both state one rule: nothing an item needs may go beyond what the student has met by that point. The kept record adds common knowledge, supplied facts and untaught response forms. The merged one adds options, hints, pointers and every path through the course, and staying vague where the order is unknown follows from that. Neither record is on record.

merges.statement: When an objective or standard spans several cases or elements, list them in the plan and give each question a different one, since material missing any one fails alignment.

folded_records.statement: When a standard lists its elements, material that claims to teach it must cover each one, and a single missing element fails its alignment.
folded_records.detail: Articles that covered only part of a standard's listed elements passed alignment (issue 341); the fix added a completeness check that sets alignment to 0.0 if any explicitly required element is entirely absent, and a proportionality check for phrases like 'various groups' (commit ee21a33 in `icloud-work/inceptbench`). The article rubric now tells the judge to list the standard's explicit elements and verify each one appears (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/article/evaluation.txt`).

merges.why: Both state one rule: every listed part of the target must be covered. One adds the planning step and a different case for each question. The other adds that one missing element fails alignment. Neither record is on record. two-of-a-kind-must-differ (on record) is about blocks repeating each other, not about coverage, so it is left as it is.

merges.statement: The skill a lesson or item claims must be one its text affords and its task really demands at the stated depth, not recall or a neighbouring skill.

folded_records.statement: Tag a lesson or question with a skill only when its text affords that skill.
folded_records.detail: Notes in a curriculum map's coverage sheet record four tag corrections (`downloads/5. Curriculum/Curriculum maps/_G3 curriculum Map.xlsx`, sheet 'SC Coverage', cells T5, K45, K52 and K96). One moves a cause-and-effect skill off a lesson whose text has no because, so or since; the other three replace tags for comparison standards that need more than one text, on lessons that work from one.

merges.why: One rule seen from two sides: a claimed skill must be one the material really exercises. Tagging only the skills the text affords is the label side of testing the skill claimed (an inference the source states outright is retrieval whatever its tag). Neither record is on record. Three nearby records each add a different check and stay apart: the-task-verb-matches-what-is-marked (the rubric), aligned-to-the-target-not-the-topic (content focus and sources) and teach-and-test-the-same-thinking (practice before the gate).

merges.statement: A marking guide describes the reasoning that earns credit in a few checks, not facts or keywords, which can be wrong or matched by an answer lacking the reasoning.

folded_records.statement: A marking guide for a written answer credits the reasoning, not key words or a growing list of accepted answers, so a right answer without that reasoning fails.
folded_records.detail: A reading course's lesson-writing playbook requires grading guidance to demand stance, not tokens: no scoring or accept spec may pass on keyword presence alone, negated, hedged or off-topic answers go to needs-work, and every quote check is an exact match that fails closed (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-course/LESSON-AUTHORING-PLAYBOOK.md`). It also forbids notes that would carry keyword-overlap scoring into another build. The guide is a small rubric of two or three checks, not words or facts to look for or an ever-growing list of accepted answers, which a pattern library in the reading project's knowledge store calls a brittle ruleset that still misses clever but correct answers (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0158-assessment-pattern-library-brainlift.qmd`). An answer that merely contains the words or facts does not pass, and neither does a right answer with missing or wrong reasoning: an AP chemistry evaluation prompt awards the point only for a correct response with a valid justification tied to the relevant principle (`shadow-bench/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/ap_chemistry_evaluation.txt`, lines 68-70).

merges.why: Both records state one rule: a marking guide sets out the reasoning that earns credit instead of listing facts or words to look for. They give two reasons for it. One says every listed fact is another chance to be wrong. The other says a keyword list passes an answer that has the words but not the reasoning. I kept the measured record because it holds the example with the failure count. Neither record was on record. I left mark-the-reasoning-not-the-outcome on its own: it says a prediction needs no correct outcome at all, and these two do not claim that.

merges.statement: Write marking criteria for each question that say exactly what earns each point, not a generic category or task-type rubric, so vague answers fail and valid wordings pass.

folded_records.statement: Write analytic marking criteria, with examples, for each question and its topic rather than generic ones for the task type, because task-specific criteria can make scoring more consistent.
folded_records.detail: The reading project's assessment pack summarises Jonsson and Svingby's 2007 review of about 75 studies on rubrics: rubric use can make scoring more consistent, especially when rubrics are analytic, specific to a task or topic, and supported with exemplars or rater training (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0153-assessment-pack-brainlift.qmd`). The benefits it reports for learning, such as clearer criteria and support for feedback and self-assessment, depended on how rubrics were used (the same file).

folded_records.statement: Each marking criterion names the specific fact an answer must meet, not a generic category.
folded_records.detail: A report on gaming the AP evaluator with short-answer items found that it accepted a 'Simply naming X without Y' template as sufficient clear criteria, even when X and Y were generic. The patch it recommended was a check that each criterion name a specific fact the example must satisfy, not a generic category. The report recommends the patch; it does not show it applied.

merges.why: All three state one rule: marking criteria are written for the particular question and say specifically what earns credit, not in generic wording. The record about naming the specific fact rests on the same finding the kept record cites: an item judge accepted generic criteria as clear ones. The task-specific record adds rubric research showing that criteria written for the question make scoring more consistent. None of the three was on record. The reasoning-not-fact-lists pair stays a separate set because naming specific facts and avoiding fact lists pull in different directions. each-part-specific-scored-on-its-own also stays separate, since it governs how a question part is built, not how its guide is written.

merges.statement: A mastery gate needs enough items to mean anything, so check what its bar demands at each test's real length: on four or five items, 90% means a perfect score.

folded_records.statement: Check what a pass mark means on a short test, where a 90% bar can demand a perfect score.
folded_records.detail: An evaluation of the live reading course in June 2026 found its 90% mastery threshold declared but not enforced, and two of its tests so short, at 4 or 5 items, that a 90% gate could only mean a perfect score. A gap analysis of the project's content-evaluation tools lists the same gate-arithmetic trap, where small tests make 90 percent require a perfect score. The project's later assessment rules define mastery through controlled evidence and downstream risk, not a global raw 90%.

merges.why: Special case: checking a short test's pass-mark arithmetic is the kept record's own step of working out what the bar demands at each test's real item count, with the same 90% example and shared evidence.

merges.statement: Make every reply depend on what the learner actually said, have each hint add what the answer lacks, and test that every branch, including 'I don't know', can fire.

folded_records.statement: Test that every branch a lesson writes can be reached by some input, above all the one for a learner who freezes.
folded_records.detail: In a Grade 3 reading course, every lesson wrote a branch for the child who freezes, with its own gentler replies, but the player classified only a tap, so a child with no answer had to guess, was classed as off track, and got the wrong conversation (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g3-reading/iteration-3/BUILD-RULES.md`; `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/course-red-team/references/finding-taxonomy.md`, section L). The rule since: when a branch is written, name the input that selects it, or it is decoration. The course standard requires every branch to be reachable in tests, from correct and partial answers to silence, error and missing data (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/student-course-quality/versions/2.0.0/GOLDEN-CHECKLIST.qmd`, Q044).

merges.why: The kept record already says every branch, the 'I don't know' one included, must be able to fire, and cites the same finding of a freeze branch that no input could reach. The other record is that clause on its own.

merges.statement: A source must be rich enough for its task, with a distinct part for each question and, when paired, distinct evidence; any false detail or failing question fails the set.

folded_records.statement: In a set of questions on a shared source, every question must pass its own checks, because one failing question can fail the whole set.
folded_records.detail: The AP evaluator's rubric for sets of choice questions on one source sets the set's factual accuracy to 0.0 if any question fails factual accuracy, and its educational accuracy to 0.0 if more than 20% of its questions fail that check. In a report on gaming that evaluator, two three-question sets scored at the 0.84 ceiling of its inferior range: the single failing critical metric was educational accuracy, driven by at least one of the three questions failing its own question-level checks.

merges.why: The kept record already says one false detail or one failing question fails the whole set, and its evidence includes a rubric where the set fails if any question fails. The other record is that clause on its own.

merges.statement: Ask a model only for the specifics a task needs, from a verified record, and have marking guides describe reasoning that earns credit rather than list facts it might invent.

folded_records.statement: A marking guide describes the reasoning that earns credit in a few checks, not facts or keywords, which can be wrong or matched by an answer lacking the reasoning.
folded_records.detail: The AP generator's system message tells it that short-answer scoring guidance describes criteria, not evidence lists (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/research/inference_clean.md`). In the failure analysis, factual accuracy caused 14 of 18 failures in one course's short-answer items, and a postmortem traced them to the guide itself: the writer filled its sample-response and acceptable-evidence fields with plausible but wrong historical examples (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/research/failure_taxonomy.md`). Every fact a guide lists, especially one its writer recalls rather than verifies, is another chance to be wrong.

merges.why: The kept record already has marking guides describe the reasoning that earns credit, for the same reason that each recalled fact is a chance to invent one. Both rest on the finding that evidence lists in scoring notes caused most factual failures. The other record is that clause in more detail.
merges.undone: by hand on 2026-10-13: a rule for marking guides and a rule for what a writer is asked for are different learnings

merges.statement: A lesson may assume only what earlier lessons taught and the learner still holds fluently, so record what each lesson assumes and adds, and check the whole sequence in code.

folded_records.statement: Record what each lesson assumes and adds, and check in code across lessons that each assumes only what earlier lessons taught.
folded_records.detail: The course evaluator spec for one course-plan program adds a lint that each lesson's assumed knowledge be a subset of what earlier lessons added, in unit order; on a demo it held across lessons l0 to l4, and a committed fixture in which lesson 2 assumes knowledge no prior lesson added fails it (`ti-courseplans-audit/docs/handoffs-2026-07-13/course-eval-layer/evaluator-spec.md`). The lesson-by-lesson evaluator scores both lessons of that fixture as fine; only the cross-lesson check separates them. The same gap covers back-references: 'as you saw last lesson' must be true against the order, and the evaluation gauntlet lints that 'last lesson' is factually last (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/train-teacher/references/gauntlet-spec.md`). The instruction-modes spec adds a fluency bar: knowledge first taught the same day, or present but not fluent, does not count as available (`ti-courseplans-audit/docs/instruction-modes-spec.md`). Tie what a lesson assumes and adds to the sentences that carry it, count only what the learner has shown, and check that the lessons meant to build on a lesson really do.

merges.why: Same rule: a lesson assumes only what earlier lessons taught and the learner showed or still holds, recorded per lesson and checked across the sequence in code. The kept record is the fuller one.

merges.statement: Assume only what every learner's path guarantees, and re-meet another subject's ideas only as that subject teaches and frames them, from a new angle, never as a first introduction.

folded_records.statement: When a lesson or text carries another subject's idea, it re-meets one that subject teaches, in that subject's words and framing, rather than introducing it first.
folded_records.detail: Guidance for the reading and writing apps, written because they cannot tell whether a student has studied a topic, makes re-encounters the goal: topics from earlier grades are fair game, same-grade topics only if the treatment works whether or not the subject lesson has happened, and each re-encounter should take a new angle while matching the subject's vocabulary, nuance and framing (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0137-science-social-studies-reencounter-guidance.qmd`). It prefers re-encountering earlier ideas to a reading or writing lesson being the first place a student meets one (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0137-science-social-studies-reencounter-guidance.qmd`), and the passage-integrity checks forbid a first introduction disguised as reading background (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/handoffs/g3-reading-v2-feedback-2026-07-16/science-passage-agent.md`). Later grades' draft ledgers are kept mainly to check whether earlier materials introduce their concepts too early (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0150-science-g6-atom-composite-ledger.qmd`).

merges.why: Both come from the same cross-subject guidance. The second half of the kept record is the other record's rule (that subject's framing, a new angle, not a repeat). The other record's 'works whether or not that lesson was taken' is the kept record's every-path rule.

merges.statement: Don't let a later step or model build on generated output, a model's own research included, until it is checked and approved, since its errors carry forward.

folded_records.statement: Don't let a later step build on generated material until that material has been checked and approved.
folded_records.detail: The instructions for building one AP unit's knowledge schema make the step that generates relationships the very last one, run after the unit's schema has been approved (`icloud-work/k_12_social_studies/ap_files/Knowledge Schema Generator - AP USH Unit 1 - Instructions.csv`). It is a written procedure; nothing here measures what building on unchecked material costs.

merges.why: Same rule in other words: no later step builds on generated material until it has been checked. The kept record is broader, since it covers models and a model's own research, and it has the measured evidence.

merges.statement: Passing items don't make a good set, lesson or course, so judge each whole on how its parts work together, taking item verdicts as given, never by adding them up.

folded_records.statement: Judge a set or lesson as a whole as well as item by item, because per-item checks can't see that every item was cloned from one template.
folded_records.detail: The quiz writer was told both to use 'the same question pattern as the example' and to be distinctly different from the previous questions, which it was shown. Each quality check was called with one question and its passage; a previous-questions text is built only in a formatter that nothing calls, and no check prompt has a slot for it. All 25 stems of the hard-level quiz use one frame ('The description/portrayal of X in paragraph(s) ... helps develop/establish the passage's ... primarily by moving from'), and no check flagged the shared frame; 24 were marked valid, and the other failed only for lacking a single correct answer. The evaluator's later set specification names template-based generation as the cause of near-duplicate stems. Judge the set on how its items work together and against each other; one lesson rubric does this and takes the per-item verdicts as given.

merges.why: Same rule at two scopes: items that each pass don't make a good set, lesson or course, so the whole is judged on how its parts work together and not by adding up item scores.

merges.statement: Sequence learning texts so knowledge recurs and builds, and seal the transfer test: never teach from it or gate progress on it, and keep its texts apart from everything taught.

folded_records.statement: Never teach from a transfer test or let it gate progress, and check that its texts share nothing with what was taught.
folded_records.detail: The practice-layer spec for one reading course defines its cold-passage benchmark as a sealed diagnostic on never-taught topics, served once, never a mastery gate and never teaching material; its first version only observes, with results going to people rather than to automatic adaptation (`ti-courseplans-audit/docs/practice-layer-spec.md`). The instruction-modes spec says the same: cold passages are never taught from (`ti-courseplans-audit/docs/instruction-modes-spec.md`). The assessment guidance requires transfer passages with zero overlap with instruction, verified, as the earlier Grade 4 and 5 cold finals had, and disjoint parallel forms (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/train-assessor/SKILL.md`).

merges.why: Same core rule: the test's texts stay unseen and apart from everything taught. The statement keeps the sequencing clause from one record and the never-a-gate clause from the other.

merges.statement: Write each question for its own text and teach no rule of thumb many texts break, such as checking the title or expecting the meaning or evidence in one sentence.

folded_records.statement: Don't teach a rule of thumb that many texts break, such as checking the main idea against the title or looking for it in one sentence.
folded_records.detail: A review rejected two pieces of main-idea advice a lesson taught: a fable's meaning is rarely contained in one sentence, and titles frequently do not state the main idea, so checking against the title is not a dependable rule. It added that the lesson might also teach that text evidence always points to one sentence, when readers often have to synthesize two ideas from different places.

merges.why: Same learning from the same feedback notes, with identical examples: checking the title or looking for one key sentence misleads because many texts break those rules. One record puts it as question writing, the other as teaching.

merges.statement: While students read, show only the text; bring questions only after the reading, take reading help away once a question appears, and let students look back at the text anytime.

folded_records.statement: Keep questions off the screen while students read, and bring a check in only after the reading stretch.
folded_records.detail: A review note said questions had been overdone to the detriment of the mental model, and a built Grade 3 lesson answered it engine-wide with story-only pages, the check appearing only after the student says they are done reading. The passage stays visible whenever a question asks the child to look back at it.

merges.why: These state the same screen rule in other words. While students read, only the text is shown. Questions come only after the reading, and the text stays available to look back at. The kept record also says to take reading help away once a question appears. I left the other pair with the folded record, against show-the-text-the-task-needs, alone: that record says the text, with the evidence part showing, sits beside any task that asks for evidence, which is a different rule from when questions appear.

merges.statement: Teach and test the combined use of skills through whole tasks that truly need them together, defined by exemplars and a rubric, because passing every part doesn't show the whole.

folded_records.statement: When a performance needs students to select, combine or justify parts, teach and gate that combined move explicitly, because a student who passes each part can still fail the whole.
folded_records.detail: The reading store's curriculum doctrine holds that students can master each knowledge component yet fail whenever they must select, combine or justify them in context, and that the gate for an integrative lesson must require the combined move rather than re-test the parts in isolation. A second round of course findings repeated it, and an evaluator gap analysis asks for tasks that coordinate several components, not only separate checks. Such whole tasks are defined by exemplars and a rubric, not by ever smaller parts (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/academics-alignment-plan.md`).

merges.why: Same learning. Both require whole tasks that need several taught skills used together, because a learner can pass each part and still fail the whole, and they share most of their evidence. One adds checking that a task called integrative really needs the combination. The other adds teaching that move explicitly and defining it by exemplars and a rubric instead of ever smaller parts. The statement keeps both. I kept the record with the measured trial and the wider evidence. Neither record was on record before this run.

merges.statement: Put an item's or a level's difficulty in the knowledge or reasoning it demands, never in labels, untaught words, hard syntax, negatives, obscure facts, padded reading or reworded easier lessons.

folded_records.statement: Make each level's lessons from that level's own sources and put the difficulty in the task, never in inflated prose or in a lower level's lesson with harder words.
folded_records.detail: A Grade 5 course's authoring rules require lessons that are genuinely Grade 5, never Grade 3 dressed up, with the complexity in the task rather than in inflated prose (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-course/LESSON-AUTHORING-PLAYBOOK.md`). A review of its lessons found one item's distractors below the grade band, readings no Grade 5 student would hold, which left the item answerable without the passage (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-course/ADVERSARIAL-REVIEW-2026-08-19.md`). A later build plan kept the rule: never a Grade 3 copy, consult the course's own sources, and log the rule behind each decision (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-book-2026-09-29/SCOUT-AND-PLAN.md`).

merges.why: One rule at two scales. Both put difficulty in the thinking a task demands, not in its language. The folded record applies this to building a harder level: it should come from that level's own sources, not be an easier lesson in harder words, which is a special case of difficulty never coming from wording. The statement names both items and levels. I kept the record with the broader evidence. Neither record was on record before this run.

merges.statement: Feedback on a wrong answer says where to look, never what the student has to produce, and only what is true of what they were given.

folded_records.statement: When a point must be learned exactly, prompt the student to produce it rather than restating it for them, since students often miss a restatement.
folded_records.detail: A research synthesis on comprehension talk notes that a recast, restating the child's idea in fuller form, keeps a conversation going, but children often do not notice it, so it does not reliably teach one specific point (Lyster and Saito 2010). Prompts, which cue the child to self-correct, more often lead to a corrected response (Lyster and Ranta 1997; Lyster and Saito 2010), so when something has to be learned exactly, prompting the child to say it again in their own words works better. The evidence is from second-language classrooms.

merges.why: prompt-rather-than-restate is a special case of the record already on file. Restating the correct form for the student tells them what they have to produce, and prompting them to produce it is what sending them back does. Its condition (a point that must be learned exactly) and its second-language classroom evidence narrow the rule but do not change it. The kept record already cites the derived rule that the app never restates the correct answer and prompts the child to say it. It was on record before this run, so it is kept and its statement stays as it is. The other records in this section were left alone because they are close but say different things. explain-the-key-and-every-wrong-option is about the explanation shown when the answer is revealed, while feedback-for-each-wrong-option is about per-option feedback after a wrong try. a-reply-that-depends-on-the-answer covers spoken or written answers, not choices. explanations-must-fit-the-item-given and shared-feedback-fits-every-answer test the truth of support text against the final item and against each answer it is shown for. correct-briefly-retest-later and short-feedback-or-fix-the-item are about the correct-test-retest cycle and length limits.

merges.statement: Fit each item's format to its target and learners: production wherever the target is to produce, and the formats of the test the course prepares for that suit their grade.

folded_records.statement: Assess a target with a format in which the learner does what it names, so have them say, write, type or draw what they must produce, explain or use.
folded_records.detail: An evaluator gap analysis for the reading project made recognition-versus-production match a binding check: a target to write, explain or draw cannot be assessed by multiple choice alone. The project's assessment rules say recognition is not enough for productive, representational, justificatory or integrative constructs, its vocabulary rules require production, and its grade-3 course judges a lesson by production (say, write, type) over selection (click). Recognising an answer or saying it is known overstates recall: about 80% of students check a word as known, about 50% can give an example and about 20% can explain it (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0121-teaching-comprehension-insights-brainlift.qmd`). A recalled term or a one-to-one match can't show an explanation: in one AP benchmark run 90% of fill-in questions failed cognitive demand, and the benchmark's report says a one-to-one matching format eliminates analytical challenge (`icloud-work/evaluator/docs/reports/BENCHMARK_RUN6_REPORT.md`; `icloud-work/evaluator/docs/reports/BENCHMARK_COMPREHENSIVE_REPORT.md`). Picking an option can't show that a learner can produce or use something.

merges.why: match-the-response-to-the-target spells out one clause of choose-the-format-the-target-needs. Both say the format must let the learner do what the target names and produce where the target is to produce. Its cases (recognition overstating recall, a recalled term or one-to-one match not showing an explanation) are instances of that clause. Neither was on record before this run. I kept choose-the-format-the-target-needs because its title, detail and example cover the whole merged statement, including the test's formats and grade fit. Every source in the other record's detail is in the evidence that folds in. response-type-before-response-count stays separate: it adds that the needed response type comes before a high response count, which neither of these says.

merges.statement: Make each question in a set and each part of a multi-part item answerable from the source and scorable alone, with none restating, revealing or depending on another's answer.

folded_records.statement: In a two-part item, the second part must not restate or reveal the first part's answer, and the first part must stand on its own.
folded_records.detail: Probes of generated items found 6 of 6 sampled two-part evidence items solvable without the passage, with the evidence part restating the first, the same cause measured at 33% gameable in the Grade 3 course (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/skills/reading-science/applied/teaching-comprehension-insights-brainlift.qmd`). In the first passage-blind solve of a Grade 5 seed bank, a two-part pair confirmed itself (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/pr-proposals/ti-courseplans-standards/staged/docs/standards/item-quality.md`), and the blind-solve build list names an evidence part restating the first as a leak to test for (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0093-evaluator-gap-analysis-inceptbench-academics-2026-07-09.qmd`). A content-integrity rule asks for one uniquely strongest evidence choice that does not reveal the first part (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/handoffs/g3-reading-v2-feedback-2026-07-16/tooling/ti-courseplans-2169d1f/skills/course-content-integrity/SKILL.md`), and the Grade 5 generator says to strengthen a first part that general knowledge can solve rather than rely on the second to rescue it (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/pr-proposals/ti-courseplans-standards/staged/courses/g5-reading/generator/G5_GENERATOR.md`). Otherwise the pair can be answered without the text.

merges.why: two-parts-neither-giving-the-other-away is the two-part case of each-part-stands-on-its-own. A second part that restates or reveals the first's answer is one part giving away another's, and a first part that stands on its own is a part answerable on its own. Neither was on record before this run. Its measured leak (sampled two-part items solvable without the passage) becomes evidence for the no-give-away clause and stays as evidence quotes, but its example field does not carry over. The kept record is contested over whether parts may build on each other, and that dispute does not touch the no-give-away clause. one-question-at-a-time stays separate: it is about showing one question per screen so the feedback can answer each part.

merges.statement: Award mastery, progress and rewards only for verified learning: passive activity, clicking through, revealed answers, guessing, replays and low-accuracy work earn nothing, and detected gaming costs points.

folded_records.statement: Give points only for verified learning: none for passive activity or low-accuracy work, and penalties rather than points for gaming.
folded_records.detail: The delivery platform the reading course runs on gives no points for passive activity until retrieval verifies learning, none below 80% accuracy, and negative points rather than zero for detected gaming (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0028-non-negotiables.qmd`, `grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0030-xp-system.qmd`). Its reason is that rewards for fake progress train students to optimise the reward system, not their knowledge (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0032-principles.qmd`). A custom reading app built on the platform was found fabricating quiz points (correct × 3, no 80% floor) and was changed to record only correctness and accuracy and leave points to the platform (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0060-incept-read-app-field-notebook.qmd`).

merges.why: Same rule in other words: only verified learning earns credit. One record names mastery, progress and rewards, with clicking through, revealed answers, guessing and replays earning nothing. The other names points, the 80% accuracy floor and penalties for gaming. Both record the same delivery app awarding quiz points with no 80% floor. Neither was on record. Left apart: the rule that preview and review controls leave learner records unchanged, including on reset. That rule is about review mode, not about what learner work earns.

merges.statement: Keep keys, rationales, rubrics and correction routes off the learner's device, even hidden, until each response is submitted, and score on the server, never trusting the screen's correctness flag.

folded_records.statement: The copy of a lesson a learner gets carries no keys, rationales, rubrics or correction routes, not even hidden, until the response each belongs to is submitted.
folded_records.detail: An AP course package builds a separate student projection that omits assessment candidates, answer keys, rationales, rubrics, feedback and correction routes, while its review projection keeps the complete evidence (`grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/courses/apush/review/evidence/case-for-review.md`). Its acceptance record says the first unit excludes keys from student HTML and withholds independent and checkpoint evidence (`grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/courses/apush/review/evidence/incept-acceptance.json`), and its assessment set withholds keys, rationales, lesson models, correction routes and retries until the relevant response is submitted (`grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/courses/apush/source/sealed-authoring/authoring/apush/canonical/unit2/assessment-set.json`).

merges.why: Same rule in other words: what reaches the learner holds only student material, and answer-bearing fields stay behind. Both cite a course package's student-only projection without keys. One adds server scoring and never trusting correctness sent from the client. The other adds rationales, rubrics, correction routes and release after submission. The statement holds both. Not folded into the older 'nothing gives the answer first', whose statement covers what is seen or heard, not hidden data or where scoring runs.

merges.statement: Everything a lesson says, quoted or not, from model answers and feedback to marking guides, must be true to its source and claim no more than the source's words support.

folded_records.statement: Every claim a lesson makes about what its text says, quoted or not, including any cause it gives, must trace to the text's own words.
folded_records.detail: An audit that checked one reading lesson against 325 rules found one critical defect: a recap shown to students gave the text a cause it never states, which the audit called the exact defect class, inference grounded in invented rather than real textual evidence, that the lesson exists to teach students to avoid. A claim-fidelity checker written for the course pulls out both quoted spans and unquoted claims introduced by 'the story says' or 'it says', the shape that hides the worst defects, since unquoted claims look like nothing. When it was recorded, the checker was not wired into any known gate. The rule covers anything a design document or knowledge base supplied, and unquoted claims are checked as strictly as quotations. A modelled inference adds only what students can be expected to know.

merges.why: Same rule: nothing a lesson says may claim more than its source supports. Both cite the same register's five feedback and reveal lines that contradict the story, and both are about an invented cause or mechanism stated as the source's. The statement keeps one record's reach (model answers, feedback, marking guides) and the other's point that unquoted claims are checked as strictly as quotes. Left apart: keeping an inference out of the text's slot and out of quote marks. That is a labelling rule, and it is contested.

merges.statement: Make the thinking a task targets, such as understanding a text rather than matching its words, impossible to skip: students take any shortcut, and a gamed pass proves nothing.

folded_records.statement: A question about a text must need the reader to understand it, not just to find words in it that match the question.
folded_records.detail: The reading project's course feedback meeting of 4 August 2026 asked that the independent text or task require genuine rereading rather than a visible word-match. The Generic Instruction BrainLift attached to a July 2026 feedback round on the course says closed-response items must require the target reasoning and must not be answerable by surface cues, keyword matching, option length or test-wise elimination.

merges.why: Special case: word-matching is one shortcut past the thinking that a question about a text targets. One of the word-matching record's two quotes is the general rule itself: closed-response items must require the target reasoning, not surface cues or keyword matching. Left apart: 'a question must need the knowledge', which adds the no-knowledge reader test and the fix, and exempts reading items. Also left apart: the older 'a question must need the text', which is about answering with no text at all.

merges.statement: A question about a text must need the text.

folded_records.statement: In a course that builds knowledge, a question on a new text must not be answerable from the earlier lessons' texts with the new text withheld.
folded_records.detail: A spine-conditioned blind solve gives the solver the earlier texts and lessons and withholds the new text. In its first run, one certified item's key was a schema generalisation the earlier lessons made derivable, so the item could not serve as evidence the student read the new text; the disposition was to exclude it, or re-author it with wrong options that fit the taught schema and that only the new text tells apart (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/artifacts/demo-unit-2026-07-10/spine-gate/SPINE-GATE-REPORT.md`, lines 81-89). A capstone gate that required a plain blind solve, a with-text control and the spine condition all to pass rejected 2 of 10 items on the spine condition alone (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/artifacts/demo-unit-2026-07-10/phase-e/capstone/gate-capstone-summary.json`). Check it by giving the solver the earlier lessons' texts and withholding the new text, not only by giving it no text at all, since what the course already taught can give later answers away.

merges.why: Special case: if the earlier lessons can answer a question on a new text with that text withheld, the question does not need the text. The older record already carries the same earlier-lessons evidence: later items must not be answerable from earlier lessons, and the same item was later solved 3 of 3 times with no text. The newer record's own counter-evidence withdraws its headline case. The older record was there before this run, so it is kept and its statement stays as it is.

merges.statement: After a miss, reteach what failed, retest on new parallel items or a fresh test form, never the same ones, check again later, and send repeated failure to placement review.

folded_records.statement: After a miss, correct it and re-test on a fresh parallel item, and cap the retries, switching to re-teaching when practice isn't working.
folded_records.detail: The reading project's course standard accepts an error path only when its trace shows correction, an alternate explanation or representation, a parallel new attempt, a delayed recheck where claimed, retry bounds and escalation after non-progress (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/student-course-quality/versions/2.0.0/GOLDEN-CHECKLIST.qmd`, Q022), and its instruction spec re-tests on a new parallel item, retests in the next dose, and sends a second consecutive failed delayed retest to placement or sequence review, never an infinite loop (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/instruction-modes-spec.md`, M7). The assessment BrainLift argues that a gate needs three outcomes, promote, keep practising or switch to corrective instruction, because without a switch persistence becomes the hidden criterion for passing, and that continued practice must widen to multiple item families (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`). A source atom from an AP U.S. History BrainLift says to reassess with a parallel task that uses different evidence (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/student-course-quality/sources/review-hub/course-insights-d7f57fb/ATOMS.json`). The fresh item shows whether the correction took. Check again later, and send a learner whose practice isn't working to re-teaching or a placement review, so that persisting on similar items never becomes the way to pass.

folded_records.statement: After a wrong answer, teach the step that failed and retry on a parallel item that uses different evidence, rather than repeating the same item.
folded_records.detail: An AP course's assessment design scores each item part by part, records the first step a learner failed, teaches through that step's local check, and gives a parallel retry with different evidence before reassessing (`grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/courses/apush/source/sealed-authoring/authoring/apush/canonical/unit2/assessment-set.json`). The package's acceptance evidence says its first unit offers targeted feedback, correction and a different-evidence retry (`grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/courses/apush/review/evidence/incept-acceptance.json`). It is a design rule in an authored course that has not yet been run with learners.

folded_records.statement: Give every gated test at least two parallel forms that share no items, so a student who retakes it meets new items rather than the same ones.
folded_records.detail: The staged assessment standard requires two parallel forms sharing zero items, so a student who retests sees the other form and no answers leak (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/pr-proposals/ti-courseplans-standards/staged/docs/standards/assessment-design.md`). Courses without them showed the problem: one re-showed the same test on a reattempt (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0022-incept-team-sync-2026-06-17.qmd`), an evaluation of a live course found no parallel forms (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0058-eval-reading-explorers-g3-allqtypes.qmd`), and a course check failed a test built as a single static form as gameable (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/BRIEFING.md`).

merges.why: All four say the same thing: after a miss, the retry or retest uses new parallel items, never the identical ones. reteach-then-retest-on-new-items and retry-on-new-items-then-re-teach say it in other words: correct or reteach, retest on fresh items, check again after a delay, and cap the retries so that repeated failure goes to a placement review instead of looping. retry-on-a-parallel-item is the single-item case without the cap. a-retake-gets-a-fresh-form is the gated-test case, where the retake comes on a parallel form that shares no items. None of the four is on_record. two-tries-then-the-answer (on_record) was left alone because it shows the answer after two tries on one check, which is a different rule.

merges.statement: Sequence the texts learners study so taught knowledge recurs and builds, and base every scored test and transfer item on unseen, unrelated texts whose answers were never taught.

folded_records.statement: Sequence learning texts so knowledge recurs and builds, and seal the transfer test: never teach from it or gate progress on it, and keep its texts apart from everything taught.
folded_records.detail: A review of the Grade 3 course called it the deepest issue with the design that its assessment passages never overlapped taught topics, so a student couldn't pass on recall but knowledge could never help either; it asked for the learning texts to be sequenced so taught knowledge recurs and compounds, with cold, non-overlapping passages kept for the test only (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0081-g3-reviewer-feedback-raw-2026-07-02-reading-explorers-v2-review-verbatim.qmd`). The project's later lessons kept both sides: an unscored on-ramp check retrieves a prior lesson's claim, while the scored items stay disjoint from that on-ramp and from every teaching claim (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0074-g3-reviewer-feedback-distilled-for-g5-2026-06-30.qmd`).

merges.why: Both state the same rule and rest on the same source quote: learning texts sequenced so knowledge recurs and builds, cold texts kept for the test, and nothing scored taken from what was taught. each-text-builds-on-the-last stays separate because it says something different: each text may need only what earlier texts added, and its test reuses the same knowledge on a new surface instead of an unrelated text.

merges.statement: Assume only what every path guarantees: each branch teaches what later content uses and agrees on facts, and topics another course teaches work in either order, from a new angle.

folded_records.statement: When a text covers a topic another subject teaches that year, make it work before or after that lesson, with a fresh angle rather than a repeat.
folded_records.detail: The reading project's cross-subject rule is to use prior-grade or sequencing-safe fresh-angle re-encounters, and to reinforce rather than redefine the other subject's framing (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0164-g3-v2-feedback-agent-routing.qmd`). Its draft science ledger adds that a same-grade reading treatment must work whether the science lesson came before or after it, and that no row of the ledger counts as proof a student has met the topic (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0149-draft-grade-5-science-ledger.qmd`).

folded_records.statement: On a branching path, every branch must teach what later pages assume and agree with the other branches on the facts.
folded_records.detail: Reviews of the dialogue branches in two Grade 3 lessons found two faults (`shadow/content-eval/reports/G3-U1-L12-review.md`, `shadow/content-eval/reports/G3-U1-L13-review.md`). In one, a word was defined on two of the five branches, so students on the other three never saw it, yet two later pages use it; in the other, a follow-up question's key contradicted what the other branches say.

merges.why: work-in-either-order is the cross-course case of the path rule: a same-year topic has to work whichever lesson comes first and takes a fresh angle instead of repeating. every-branch-teaches-what-follows is the branching case: later pages may use only what every branch taught. assume-only-what-was-taught-and-kept stays separate because it adds a different test, knowledge still held fluently on a later day and checked across the sequence in code.

merges.statement: Teach confusable ideas as a pair: start with clear-cut examples that tell them apart, keep borderline cases for later, contrast them explicitly, and mix them only once both are learned.

folded_records.statement: When students first meet a distinction, use only clear-cut cases that carry a visible marker, and keep borderline cases for later.
folded_records.detail: Both persuasive-text lesson designs in a Grade 3 unit check their fact and opinion sorts in an accuracy sweep. In the first, each fact sentence is checkable, each opinion sentence carries a feeling-word, and no borderline cases are used at first exposure; the second, the unit's other persuasion lesson, keeps borderline cases out of its modelled step.

merges.why: clear-cut-cases-first is the first-examples clause of the confusable-pairs rule applied to one distinction: the first cases plainly tell the two sides apart and borderline ones come later. The fact and opinion distinction it uses is one of the pairs that record already lists. teach-the-general-case-first and teach-it-right-the-first-time say different things and are left alone.
